5.text: “two-sided levirate,”³ in which the widow must marry the younger brother,

6.text: younger cousin, or sister’s or brother’s son, of her deceased husband; and

7.text: the widower must marry the younger sister, younger cousin, or sister’s or

17.text: MARRIAGE AMONG THE MARITIME CHUKCHEE. — My information in regard

18.text: to marriage among the Maritime Chukchee is rather scanty. On the whole,

19.text: however, I can say that the basis of marital union among the Maritime

20.text: Chukchee and the Asiatic Eskimo is the same as among the Reindeer Chuk-

21.text: chee. We find again marriages of near relatives; marriages through exchange

22.text: between families, woman for woman; and, finally, marriages into a strange

23.text: family after a term of service. A young Maritime Chukchee or Eskimo

24.text: enters the service of his prospective father-in-law, and lives with him for two

25.text: or three years, giving him the products of his labor, until the father finally

26.text: consents to give him the bride. If the bride is too young to enter the mari-

27.text: tal union, the groom must live with his father-in-law, work diligently, and

28.text: wait until the bride grows up and matures. A number of my native friends

29.text: of Maritime Chukchee extraction once enumerated and estimated the value of

30.text: the products of their chase which each had given to his father-in-law while

31.text: serving for the bride. In this enumeration, seals, walruses, fish, and even

32.text: whales (whalebone excepted), were not mentioned at all, being classed as food

33.text: good only for home consumption. The list contained merely those products

34.text: which could be sold to whalers or exchanged with Reindeer Chukchee. One

35.text: said, “During the entire time, I gave to my father-in-law three strips of whale-

36.text: bone, five white foxes, five large reindeer-skins, ten pairs of walrus-tusks.”
